title: Dynamical axion quasiparticles: an open quantum system
abstract: We study the non-equilibrium dynamics of emergent dynamical axion quasiparticles (DAQ) coupled to a photon bath in equilibrium via a Chern-Simons term as a quantum open system. A quantum master equation (QME) is derived up to second order in this coupling implementing only a \emph{partial} Markov approximation, allowing time dependent rates in the Lindblad (QME). These are determined by the equilibrium correlation functions of the Chern-Simons density, and their time dependence allows us to explore transient dynamics in coherences and population: the formation of the quasiparticle on short time scales and its decay, and the build-up of population with an effective time dependent rate. Early time evolution features quantum \emph{anti} Zeno dynamics with enhanced quasiparticle decay and population growth. These phenomena describe transient violations of Fermi's Golden rule and of \emph{detailed balance}, and are distinct \emph{non-Markovian} effects directly related to the spectral density of the Chern-Simons correlators. We obtain the equation of motion of coherent (DAQ) condensates both with the (QME) and with quantum many body linear response establishing a direct bridge between both methods. As a corollary we obtain the expectation value of the Chern-Simons density \emph{induced} by a (DAQ) condensate in linear response, the topological susceptibility is shown to be proportional to the (DAQ) many body self-energy. We provide a Feynman diagram-based interpretation of approximations invoked in the (QME) and corrections from system-bath correlations in higher order.
summary: The paper analyzes the time evolution of dynamical axion quasiparticles coupled to a photon bath using open quantum system formalisms. By deriving and comparing results from a Quantum Master Equation (QME) with those from quantum many-body linear response, it reveals non-Markovian transient effects like anti-Zeno dynamics. This work provides a unified theoretical framework for understanding dissipation in topological materials.
main_problem: The study investigates the non-equilibrium dynamics of emergent dynamical axion quasiparticles (DAQ) coupled to a photon bath via a Chern-Simons term, treating it as an open quantum system.
main_result: The analysis establishes a direct bridge between the Quantum Master Equation (QME) approach and quantum many-body linear response theory, revealing transient non-Markovian effects like anti-Zeno dynamics.
method: The authors derive and analyze the time evolution using a QME derived with only a partial Markov approximation, comparing it rigorously to results from quantum many-body linear response theory.
model_or_system: The system involves DAQ quasiparticles coupled to an electromagnetic bath via a Chern-Simons term. The dynamics are modeled by deriving and solving the reduced density matrix evolution equation (QME).
key_observables: Coherences, population of the DAQ condensate, topological susceptibility ($\chi_t$), and the expectation value of the induced Chern-Simons density.
important_parameters: Transient time scales are crucial; early time dynamics exhibit quantum anti-Zeno effects, violating Fermi's Golden rule and detailed balance.
main_assumptions: The primary approximations include using a partial Markov approximation in the QME and assuming weak coupling ($g^2$ order) when applying factorization techniques from linear response theory.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the time evolution of rate integrals, showing the transition from early-time oscillatory behavior to long-time secular growth consistent with different theoretical limits.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first setting up the open quantum system framework (QME), then deriving equivalent equations using linear response theory, and finally analyzing the resulting time evolution in multiple regimes (transient vs. long-time) to confirm consistency across methods.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it tackles non-equilibrium dynamics in topological systems by bridging two powerful theoretical tools—open quantum system master equations and many-body linear response theory—to study transient phenomena.
